introduction to physics.definition: Physics is the branch of science that studies matter, energy, motion and their interactions.
notes: Physics explains natural phenomena.
Physics uses experiments and observations.
SI units are used in measurements.

worked_examples.question: Name two branches of Physics.
worked_examples.solution: Mechanics and Optics.

practice_questions: Define Physics.
State two applications of Physics.
answers: Physics is the study of matter, energy and their interactions.
Engineering and medicine.

measurement i.definition: Measurement is the process of determining the magnitude of a physical quantity.
notes: Length is measured in metres.
Mass is measured in kilograms.
Time is measured in seconds.
practice_questions: State the SI unit of length.
answers: metre (m)

measurement ii.definition: Measurement II covers area, volume and density.
notes: Area is measured in square metres.
Volume is measured in cubic metres.
Density is mass per unit volume.

worked_examples.question: Find the density of a body of mass 20 kg and volume 5 m³.
worked_examples.solution: Density = 20 ÷ 5 = 4 kg/m³.

practice_questions: Define density.
answers: Density is mass per unit volume.

force.definition: A force is a push or pull acting on an object.
notes: Force changes motion.
The SI unit is Newton.

worked_examples.question: A 5 kg object accelerates at 2 m/s².

practice_questions: Define force.
answers: A force is a push or pull acting on an object.

pressure.definition: Pressure is force per unit area.
notes: Pressure increases when area decreases.
SI unit is Pascal.

worked_examples.question: 100 N acts on 5 m².
worked_examples.solution: Pressure = 20 Pa.

practice_questions: State the formula for pressure.
answers: P = F / A.

particulate nature of matter.definition: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. It is made up of tiny particles called atoms and molecules.
notes: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas.
Particles are always in constant random motion.
Particles in solids are closely packed.
Particles in liquids can move past one another.
Particles in gases are far apart and move freely.
Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.
Brownian motion is evidence that particles are constantly moving.
Heating increases the kinetic energy of particles.

worked_examples.question: Why does the smell of perfume spread throughout a room?
worked_examples.solution: Perfume particles diffuse through the air from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.

worked_examples.question: Why does sugar dissolve faster in hot water?
worked_examples.solution: The particles move faster at higher temperatures, increasing the rate of diffusion.

practice_questions: Define matter.
State the three states of matter.
Define diffusion.
Explain Brownian motion.
Why is diffusion faster in gases than in liquids?
State two differences between solids and gases.
Give two examples of diffusion.
Why do gases occupy the whole container?
answers: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass.
Solid, liquid and gas.
Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.
Brownian motion is the random movement of tiny particles suspended in a fluid.
Because gas particles move faster and are further apart.
Solids have fixed shape and volume while gases have neither.
Perfume spreading and ink spreading in water.
Because gas particles move freely in all directions.

thermal expansion.definition: Thermal expansion is the increase in the length, area or volume of a substance when it is heated.
notes: Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled.
Expansion occurs because particles gain kinetic energy and move further apart.
Solids expand less than liquids, while gases expand the most.
Expansion can be linear, superficial (area) or cubical (volume).
Expansion joints are left on bridges and railway lines.
Electric power lines are left slightly loose to allow expansion.
Bimetallic strips are used in thermostats.
Thermometers work because liquids expand when heated.
Glass may crack if heated unevenly.
Thermal expansion has both advantages and disadvantages.

worked_examples.question: Why are gaps left between railway rails?
worked_examples.solution: They allow the rails to expand during hot weather and prevent buckling.

worked_examples.question: Why do overhead electric cables sag more on hot days?
worked_examples.solution: The cables expand when heated, increasing their length.

worked_examples.question: Why is a bimetallic strip used in an electric iron?
worked_examples.solution: It bends when heated and automatically switches the iron on or off.

State one advantage and one disadvantage of thermal expansion.
answers: Thermal expansion is the increase in size of a substance when heated.
Thermometers, bimetallic strips and expansion joints.
Buckling of railway lines and cracking of glass.
To allow the bridge to expand safely.
Because the wires expand when heated.
The two metals expand at different rates causing the strip to bend.
Linear, superficial and cubical expansion.
Uneven expansion creates stress which cracks the glass.
Thermometer and thermostat.
Advantage: Used in thermometers. Disadvantage: Can buckle railway lines.

heat transfer.definition: Heat transfer is the movement of heat energy from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.
notes: Heat always flows from a hotter body to a colder body.
There are three methods of heat transfer: conduction, convection and radiation.
Conduction mainly occurs in solids.
Convection occurs in liquids and gases.
Radiation does not require a material medium.
Metals are good conductors of heat.
Wood, plastic and rubber are poor conductors (insulators).
Black dull surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of heat.
Shiny silver surfaces are poor absorbers but good reflectors of heat.
Vacuum flasks reduce heat transfer by conduction, convection and radiation.

worked_examples.question: Why are saucepan handles made of plastic?
worked_examples.solution: Plastic is a poor conductor of heat, preventing heat from reaching the hand.

worked_examples.question: Why are cooking pots made of aluminium?
worked_examples.solution: Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, allowing food to cook quickly.

worked_examples.question: Why is the inside of a vacuum flask silvered?
worked_examples.solution: To reflect thermal radiation and reduce heat loss.

Radiation.
Because they contain free electrons that transfer heat quickly.
Wood and plastic.
To allow hot air to escape.
Sea breeze is formed by convection currents due to unequal heating of land and sea.
Cooking utensils, electric irons and soldering irons.
Because black surfaces absorb heat more efficiently.

temperature.definition: Temperature is the measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
notes: Temperature determines the direction of heat flow.
Heat flows from a body at a higher temperature to one at a lower temperature.
Temperature is measured using a thermometer.
The SI unit of temperature is Kelvin (K).
The Celsius scale (°C) is commonly used.
The freezing point of pure water is 0°C.
The boiling point of pure water is 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
Normal human body temperature is approximately 37°C.
Clinical thermometers measure body temperature.
Laboratory thermometers measure temperatures in experiments.

answers: Temperature is the measure of the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.
Kelvin (K).
Heat is energy while temperature measures hotness or coldness.
Clinical thermometer and laboratory thermometer.
To measure temperatures during scientific experiments and laboratory investigations.

electrostatics i.definition: Electrostatics is the study of electric charges at rest.
notes: There are two types of electric charges: positive and negative.
Like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
Electric charges are produced by friction.
Materials that easily gain or lose electrons become charged.
Conductors allow electric charges to flow easily.
Insulators do not allow electric charges to flow easily.
Charging can occur by friction, contact or induction.
Lightning is a natural example of static electricity.
Earthing removes excess electric charge safely.
Electroscopes are used to detect electric charges.

worked_examples.question: A plastic ruler is rubbed with dry hair. What happens?
worked_examples.solution: The ruler becomes negatively charged due to friction.

worked_examples.question: Why is lightning dangerous?
worked_examples.solution: It is a large discharge of static electricity carrying enormous energy.

worked_examples.question: Why are fuel tankers fitted with metal chains?
worked_examples.solution: The chains earth the tanker and prevent sparks caused by static electricity.

Positive and negative charges.
Like charges repel while unlike charges attract.
Rubbing transfers electrons from one material to another.
Friction, contact and induction.
Conductors allow charges to move while insulators do not.
Photocopiers, spray painting and electrostatic precipitators.

It safely removes excess electric charge.

cells and simple circuits.definition: An electric cell is a source of electrical energy that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. A simple circuit is a complete path through which electric current flows.
notes: A simple circuit consists of a cell, connecting wires, a switch and a load such as a bulb.
Current flows only in a closed circuit.
Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
Electrons flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
Cells may be connected in series or parallel.
Dry cells are primary cells and cannot be recharged.
Accumulators are secondary cells and can be recharged.
A switch opens or closes a circuit.
Conductors allow current to pass while insulators do not.
Circuit diagrams use standard electrical symbols.

worked_examples.question: Why does a bulb fail to light in an open circuit?
worked_examples.solution: Because the circuit is incomplete and current cannot flow.

worked_examples.question: Name two components required to make a simple electric circuit.
worked_examples.solution: A cell and connecting wires.

worked_examples.question: State the direction of conventional current.
worked_examples.solution: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal.

current electricity.definition: Current electricity is the continuous flow of electric charges through a conductor in a closed circuit.
notes: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
Current is measured using an ammeter connected in series.
Potential difference (voltage) is measured using a voltmeter connected in parallel.
Resistance is the opposition to the flow of electric current.
Ohm's Law states that current is directly proportional to voltage provided temperature remains constant.
Conductors have low resistance while insulators have very high resistance.
Resistance increases with the length of a conductor.
Resistance decreases when the cross-sectional area increases.
Electrical energy is converted into heat, light or mechanical energy.
A fuse protects electrical appliances from excessive current.

Ampere (A).

magnetism.definition: Magnetism is the property of certain materials to attract iron, nickel, cobalt and steel.
notes: A magnet has two poles: North and South.
Like poles repel while unlike poles attract.
Magnetic materials include iron, nickel, cobalt and steel.
Non-magnetic materials include wood, plastic, glass and copper.
A freely suspended magnet points in the North-South direction.
Magnetic field lines run from the North pole to the South pole outside a magnet.
The magnetic field is strongest at the poles.
Magnets can be made by stroking, electrical method or induction.
Magnets can lose magnetism by heating, hammering or improper storage.
Magnets should be stored with soft iron keepers.

worked_examples.question: A freely suspended magnet is left to settle. In which direction will it point?
worked_examples.solution: It points in the North-South direction.

worked_examples.question: Name two magnetic materials.
worked_examples.solution: Iron and steel.

worked_examples.question: Why are keepers used when storing magnets?
worked_examples.solution: They reduce loss of magnetism.

Heating, hammering and placing in an alternating magnetic field.

Electric motors and loudspeakers.
To reduce loss of magnetism.

floating and sinking.definition: Floating and sinking depend on the upthrust acting on a body and its weight.
notes: Upthrust is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed body.
A body floats if the upthrust is equal to or greater than its weight.
A body sinks if its weight is greater than the upthrust.
Archimedes' Principle states that a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
Density determines whether an object floats or sinks.
Objects less dense than water float.
Objects denser than water sink.
Ships float because they displace a large volume of water.
Submarines control floating and sinking using ballast tanks.
Hydrometers are used to measure the relative density of liquids.

worked_examples.question: A wooden block is placed in water and floats. Why?
worked_examples.solution: Its density is less than that of water, so the upthrust balances its weight.

worked_examples.question: Why does a stone sink in water?
worked_examples.solution: Its density is greater than that of water, so its weight is greater than the upthrust.

worked_examples.question: State Archimedes' Principle.
worked_examples.solution: A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.

waves.definition: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one point to another without transferring matter.
notes: Waves transfer energy but not matter.
There are two main types of waves: transverse waves and longitudinal waves.
In transverse waves, particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of wave travel.
In longitudinal waves, particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel.
Examples of transverse waves include light waves and water waves.
Examples of longitudinal waves include sound waves.
The highest point of a transverse wave is called a crest.
The lowest point of a transverse wave is called a trough.
Wavelength is the distance between two successive crests or troughs.
Frequency is the number of complete waves produced per second.
The period is the time taken to produce one complete wave.
Wave speed depends on the medium through which the wave travels.

Transverse waves vibrate at right angles while longitudinal waves vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.

sound waves.definition: Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrating bodies and transmitted through a material medium as longitudinal waves.
notes: Sound requires a material medium to travel.
Sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound waves are longitudinal waves.
The speed of sound is greatest in solids, lower in liquids and lowest in gases.
The speed of sound in air at room temperature is about 340 m/s.
The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency.
The loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude.
Echoes are produced when sound is reflected from a surface.
Reverberation is the persistence of sound due to repeated reflections.
Ultrasound has frequencies above 20,000 Hz.
The human ear hears frequencies between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz.

magnetic effect of electric current.definition: The magnetic effect of electric current is the production of a magnetic field around a conductor carrying electric current.
notes: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field.
The direction of the magnetic field is determined using the right-hand grip rule.
The magnetic field around a straight conductor is circular.
The magnetic field inside a solenoid is uniform.
A solenoid behaves like a bar magnet.
An electromagnet is produced when current flows through a coil wound around a soft iron core.
The strength of an electromagnet depends on the current, the number of turns and the core material.
Soft iron is used because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised.
Electromagnets are stronger than permanent magnets.
Electromagnets are widely used in industry.

electromagnetic induction.definition: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force (e.m.f.) in a conductor when there is a change in magnetic flux linking the conductor.
notes: Electromagnetic induction was discovered by Michael Faraday.
An induced current flows only when there is relative motion between a magnet and a conductor.
No current is induced if there is no change in magnetic flux.
The direction of the induced current is determined using Fleming's Right-Hand Rule.
The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. increases with the speed of motion.
Increasing the number of turns of the coil increases the induced e.m.f.
Using a stronger magnet increases the induced e.m.f.
Generators work using electromagnetic induction.
Transformers also depend on electromagnetic induction.

worked_examples.solution: Move the magnet faster and increase the number of turns of the coil.

worked_examples.question: Why is no current produced when the magnet is stationary inside the coil?
worked_examples.solution: Because there is no change in magnetic flux.

mains electricity.definition: Mains electricity is the electrical energy supplied to homes, schools and industries through the national power grid.

Alternating current changes direction continuously.
Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only.
The three wires in domestic wiring are the live wire, neutral wire and earth wire.
The live wire is usually brown, the neutral wire is blue and the earth wire is green/yellow.
A fuse protects electrical appliances by melting when excessive current flows.
A circuit breaker automatically disconnects the supply during overloads or short circuits.
The earth wire protects users from electric shock.
Electrical power is measured in watts (W) while electrical energy is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh).
One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1000 W appliance operating for one hour.

x-rays.definition: X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic waves with very short wavelengths and high penetrating power.

They travel at the speed of light.
They have very short wavelengths and high frequencies.
X-rays are produced when fast-moving electrons strike a metal target.
They are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

radioactivity.definition: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei accompanied by the emission of alpha, beta or gamma radiation.
notes: Radioactivity was discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896.
Marie and Pierre Curie discovered radioactive elements such as radium and polonium.
Radioactive decay is spontaneous and cannot be controlled.
There are three main types of radiation: alpha, beta and gamma.
Alpha particles have the highest ionising power but the lowest penetrating power.
Beta particles have moderate ionising and penetrating power.
Gamma rays have the greatest penetrating power but the lowest ionising power.
Radioactivity is measured using a Geiger-Müller (GM) tube and counter.
Half-life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei to decay.
Radioactive materials must be handled carefully using lead shielding and remote handling equipment.
formulae: Half-life = Time taken for half the radioactive nuclei to decay

worked_examples.question: A radioactive substance has a half-life of 8 days. If the initial mass is 80 g, what mass remains after 16 days?
worked_examples.solution: After one half-life: 40 g. After two half-lives: 20 g.

worked_examples.question: Which radiation can be stopped by paper?
worked_examples.solution: Alpha radiation.

worked_examples.question: Which radiation has the highest penetrating power?
worked_examples.solution: Gamma radiation.

answers: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of unstable nuclei accompanied by emission of radiation.
Alpha, beta and gamma.
Alpha has high ionising but low penetrating power; beta has moderate ionising and penetrating power; gamma has low ionising but high penetrating power.

electronics.definition: Electronics is the branch of physics that deals with the control and movement of electrons in electronic devices and circuits.
notes: Electronic devices control the flow of electrons.
Semiconductors include silicon and germanium.
A diode allows current to flow in only one direction.
A light emitting diode (LED) produces light when current flows through it.
A transistor is used as an amplifier or switch.
A resistor limits the flow of electric current.
A capacitor stores electrical charge temporarily.
An integrated circuit (IC) contains many electronic components on a single chip.
Electronic circuits are used in radios, televisions, computers and mobile phones.
Digital electronics uses binary numbers (0 and 1).

worked_examples.question: What is the function of a diode?
worked_examples.solution: A diode allows current to flow in one direction only.

worked_examples.question: State one use of a transistor.
worked_examples.solution: It is used as an amplifier or an electronic switch.

worked_examples.question: Why are LEDs preferred to filament bulbs?
worked_examples.solution: They consume less power, last longer and produce less heat.

answers: Electronics is the study of the control of electrons in electronic devices.
A semiconductor is a material whose conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator.

It stores electric charge temporarily.

circular motion.definition: Circular motion is the motion of a body along a circular path about a fixed centre.
notes: In uniform circular motion, speed remains constant but velocity changes continuously.
A force directed towards the centre of the circle keeps the body moving in a circular path.
This force is called centripetal force.
Centrifugal force is an apparent outward force observed in a rotating frame.
Examples of circular motion include satellites orbiting the Earth, a stone tied to a string and vehicle wheels.
Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement.
One complete revolution is equal to 360° or 2π radians.
The period is the time taken to complete one revolution.
Frequency is the number of revolutions per second.
Banking roads reduces the risk of vehicles skidding while negotiating bends.

worked_examples.question: A stone of mass 2 kg moves in a circle of radius 5 m at 10 m/s. Find the centripetal force.
A wheel makes 4 revolutions every second. Find its frequency.
worked_examples.solution: Frequency = 4 Hz.

worked_examples.question: A body completes one revolution in 0.5 s. Find its frequency.

Centripetal force is the force directed towards the centre of a circular path.

gravitation.definition: Gravitation is the force of attraction between any two masses in the universe.
notes: Every object with mass attracts every other object.
Gravity is the force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth.
The acceleration due to gravity on Earth is approximately 9.8 m/s² (often taken as 10 m/s² in KCSE calculations).
Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body.
Mass is the amount of matter in a body and remains constant.
Weight changes depending on the value of gravity.
The universal law of gravitation was stated by Sir Isaac Newton.
Satellites remain in orbit because of gravitational attraction.
The Moon revolves around the Earth due to gravity.
Gravitational force decreases as the distance between two bodies increases.

worked_examples.question: Calculate the weight of a body of mass 12 kg. (g = 10 m/s²)

worked_examples.solution: Mass = Weight ÷ g = 250 ÷ 10 = 25 kg.

worked_examples.question: Why do astronauts appear weightless in orbit?
worked_examples.solution: They are in continuous free fall around the Earth.

Mass is the amount of matter while weight is the force due to gravity.
Every two bodies attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Newton (N).

electrostatics ii.definition: Electrostatics II deals with electric fields, electric potential, capacitors and the applications of static electricity.
notes: An electric field is the region around a charged body where another charge experiences a force.
Electric field lines originate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges.
Electric field lines never cross one another.
The strength of an electric field is greatest where the field lines are closest together.
Capacitors are devices used to store electric charge.
Capacitance is the ability of a capacitor to store charge.
The SI unit of capacitance is the Farad (F).
Lightning conductors protect buildings from lightning strikes.
Electrostatic precipitators remove dust particles from industrial gases.
Static electricity is used in spray painting and photocopiers.

electromagnetic spectrum.definition: The electromagnetic spectrum is the complete range of electromagnetic waves arranged according to wavelength or frequency.
notes: Electromagnetic waves do not require a material medium.
They all travel through a vacuum at a speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
They are transverse waves.
The electromagnetic spectrum consists of radio waves, microwaves, infrared rays, visible light, ultraviolet rays, X-rays and gamma rays.
Radio waves have the longest wavelength and lowest frequency.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.
Visible light is the only part of the spectrum that can be detected by the human eye.
The colours of visible light are Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo and Violet (ROYGBIV).
The frequency of electromagnetic waves increases from radio waves to gamma rays.
The wavelength decreases from radio waves to gamma rays.

worked_examples.solution: Gamma rays.
